title: IELTS Speaking Part 2: The Cue-Card Long Turn
summary: How to use your 1-minute prep and talk for a full 1–2 minutes on the cue card without drying up.

nodes.label: 1 minute prep
nodes.note: Jot keywords for each bullet — not full sentences

nodes.label: Cover the bullets
nodes.note: Touch every prompt on the card, in order

nodes.label: Extend with tenses
nodes.note: Past → present → future keeps you talking

nodes.label: Finish with feeling
nodes.note: End on why it mattered / how you felt

chunks.heading: Use your one minute — write keywords, not sentences
chunks.body: After the examiner hands you the task card you get **one minute** to prepare and can make notes. Jot a **keyword for each bullet point**, not full sentences — you won't have time to read them out anyway.
chunks.realExample: Card: 'Describe a journey you enjoyed.' Notes: 'train → Goa → w/ cousins → missed stop, laughed → felt free'. Five words become a two-minute talk.
chunks.memoryHook: One word per bullet. Notes are a launch pad, not a script.

chunks.heading: Answer every bullet on the card
chunks.body: The card gives a topic and **three or four prompts** ('who', 'where', 'why'). Walk through them **in order** so you never run out of things to say and the examiner hears full coverage.
chunks.realExample: 'Describe a person who inspired you' with who / how you met / what they did / why they inspired you → just answer those four in turn and you've built the whole talk.
chunks.memoryHook: The bullets ARE your paragraph plan. Follow them top to bottom.

chunks.heading: Extend with stories and tenses
chunks.body: You must speak for **1 to 2 minutes** with no interruption. Stretch each point using **time**: what it was like before (past), how it is now (present), what you hope next (future). Small details and feelings fill time naturally.
chunks.realExample: Instead of 'I like my bike,' say: 'I saved for months to buy it (past), I now ride it everywhere (present), and I'm planning a coastal trip next summer (future).' One object, three tenses, thirty seconds.
chunks.memoryHook: Past–Present–Future: the time-travel trick that never dries up.

chunks.heading: Don't stop early — keep going until told
chunks.body: Part 2 is a **monologue**. Keep talking until the examiner says 'thank you'; stopping at 40 seconds hurts your Fluency score. If you finish the bullets, add why it mattered or how you felt.
chunks.realExample: Ran out after the facts? Add: 'Looking back, that trip is when I realised I love travelling alone — it still shapes the choices I make today.' A reflective ending buys you the last 20 seconds.
chunks.memoryHook: Silence is the enemy. When in doubt, add a feeling.

recall.q: How long do you get to prepare in Speaking Part 2, and can you write notes?
recall.a: One minute to prepare, and yes — you may make notes on the paper provided.

recall.q: How long should you speak in the Part 2 long turn?
recall.a: Between 1 and 2 minutes, without interruption, until the examiner stops you.

recall.q: What should your prep-minute notes look like?
recall.a: One keyword per bullet point, not full sentences — a launch pad, not a script.

recall.q: What is a reliable way to extend your answer and avoid drying up?
recall.a: Use tenses — describe the past, the present and the future of the topic — and add small details and feelings.

recall.q: Why shouldn't you stop speaking as soon as you've covered the facts?
recall.a: It's a monologue assessed partly on fluency; stopping early loses time, so add why it mattered or how you felt until the examiner says thank you.
